parts.name: Top
notes: The face shown is the top surface; its dadoes are in the underside.

parts.name: Case bottom
notes: The face shown is its top face, with the dadoes; it is the floor of every bay.

parts.name: Left side
notes: Its dadoes face right, into the cabinet.

parts.name: Right side
notes: Its dadoes face left, into the cabinet.

parts.name: Partition
notes: Dadoes on both faces, opposite each other. It stops behind the doors’ tracks.

parts.name: Back rail
notes: Under the top at the back of its bay, its ends in the back of the dadoes.

parts.name: Leg
notes: Its two tapered faces and its two mortises face into the cabinet; the foot is the first end.

parts.name: Front and back apron
notes: A tenon at each end goes into a leg; miter the tenons’ ends where two meet inside it.

parts.name: Side apron
notes: A tenon at each end goes into a leg; miter the tenons’ ends where two meet inside it.

parts.name: Cleat
notes: Glued to the inside of a side apron, flush with its top; the case bottom is screwed down through it.
Each slot is 1/4" longer than its round hole: the case bottom's movement across its 17" depth, from the species and moisture range, plus 1/16".

parts.name: Outer stile
notes: The door’s outer edge, against its side when the door is closed, with the finger recess in its front face.

parts.name: Inner stile
notes: The door’s edge that runs past the partition.

parts.name: Door rail
notes: A stub tenon at each end fits the stiles’ grooves. Each door’s bottom rail runs in the bottom track and its top rail in the top track.

parts.name: Door panel
notes: Its grain runs up and down. Rabbeted on both faces at every edge, to a tongue that fits the grooves.
It floats in its grooves, unglued, with 1/8" at each edge across its grain: half its movement across 14-1/2", from the species and moisture range, plus 1/32".
Finish it before the frame is glued around it, so no bare wood shows at its edges when it shrinks.

hardware.name: Wood screws
notes: Long enough to pass through a cleat and about two-thirds of the way into the case bottom, but not out its top. Confirm the size with an experienced builder.

hardware.name: Wood glue
notes: Enough for every panel glue-up and every dado joint.

hardware.name: Finish
notes: Choose it with an experienced builder, and follow its instructions for ventilation.

hardwareNotes: Every joint is glued but the case bottom, which is screwed to the base through slotted holes so it can move, and the door panels, which float in their frames.
To put a door in, lift it up into the top track, swing its bottom in, and drop it into the bottom track: the left door in the front track and the right door in the back one.

inputs.label: Breadth
inputs.basis: One board, as thick as the board stock, from the template

inputs.label: Depth
inputs.basis: One board, as thick as the board stock, from the template

inputs.label: Half of the records and of everything on the top, per inch of apron, over the span
Length of records, along every bay
Modulus of elasticity, Cherry, black, clear wood at 12% moisture content

sources.locator: Chapter 5, Table 5-3b, notes a and c, p. 5-13

inputs.label: Creep factor, seasoned lumber in dry service

assumptions: Each apron is a simply supported span between its legs; the mortises and tenons hold its ends but are taken as pinned.
Records fill every bay, and the case bottom passes their weight and everything on the top to the front and back aprons equally.
Taking the apron alone ignores the case bottom and sides above it, which stiffen it, so this overstates the sag.
Simply supported between the two supports.
E is the average for small, clear, straight-grained specimens; boards with knots or cross grain may be less stiff.
E includes shear deflection, so bending deflection alone is computed.
E is at 12% moisture content; most properties increase as wood dries below that, so drier indoor wood is stiffer.
No NDS adjustment factors apply to a clear-wood value.
formulas: For each load P at a (b = L − a): δ(x) = P·b·x·(L² − b² − x²) / (6·E·I·L) for x ≤ a, mirrored for x ≥ a
For the uniform load w: δ(x) = w·x·(L³ − 2·L·x² + x³) / (24·E·I)
Δ_T(x) = K_cr · Δ_LT(x) + Δ_ST(x); δ = largest Δ_T over the span

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether 3/8" of wood between each partition's back-to-back dadoes holds the back rails.
flags.why: Dadoes 3/16" deep on both faces of a 3/4" partition leave 3/8" between them, and no source gives a limit.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether the back rails, glued into dadoes with their grain across the sides’ grain, will let the sides move.
flags.why: The sides move front to back with the seasons; a rail glued across them resists it at the back corners. The Wood Movement section estimates how much.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder to look over the base under a full load of records, and the top under everything that stands on it.
flags.why: Records are heavy and stay for years, and Kerf computes only the long aprons’ and the top’s sag.

checklist.confirm: Confirm with an experienced builder that the dadoes and back rails keep the case square under a sideways push.
checklist.why: An open back has no panel to stop the case racking.

checklist.confirm: Confirm whether the cabinet, loaded with records and with everything on the top, can tip forward.
checklist.why: It is low and deep, but a heavy top load and a pull on the front can still tip a cabinet.

checklist.confirm: Confirm with an experienced builder that the mortise-and-tenon joints keep the base square and steady under a sideways push.
checklist.why: Short legs and aprons are a common, proven base, but Kerf does not compute joint strength.

checklist.confirm: Confirm with an experienced builder how strong the glued dado joints are for this load.
checklist.why: Kerf does not compute joint strength.

checklist.element: Bending and shear of the aprons and top
checklist.confirm: Confirm the aprons and top are strong enough, not only stiff enough.
checklist.why: There are no published design values for furniture lumber, so Kerf checks only deflection.

E is the average for small, clear, straight-grained specimens; boards with knots or cross grain may be less stiff.
E includes shear deflection, so bending deflection alone is computed.
E is at 12% moisture content; most properties increase as wood dries below that, so drier indoor wood is stiffer.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether 1/2" of wood between each partition's back-to-back dadoes holds the back rails.
flags.why: Dadoes 1/4" deep on both faces of a 1" partition leave 1/2" between them, and no source gives a limit.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder whether the back rails, glued into dadoes with their grain across the sides’ grain, will let the sides move.
flags.why: The sides move front to back with the seasons; a rail glued across them resists it at the back corners. The Wood Movement section estimates how much.

flags.ask: Ask an experienced builder to look over the base under a full load of records, and the top under everything that stands on it.
flags.why: Records are heavy and stay for years, and Kerf computes only the long aprons’ and the top’s sag.

checklist.confirm: Confirm with an experienced builder that the dadoes and back rails keep the case square under a sideways push.
checklist.why: An open back has no panel to stop the case racking.

checklist.confirm: Confirm whether the cabinet, loaded with records and with everything on the top, can tip forward.
checklist.why: It is low and deep, but a heavy top load and a pull on the front can still tip a cabinet.

checklist.confirm: Confirm with an experienced builder that the mortise-and-tenon joints keep the base square and steady under a sideways push.
checklist.why: Short legs and aprons are a common, proven base, but Kerf does not compute joint strength.

checklist.confirm: Confirm with an experienced builder how strong the glued dado joints are for this load.
checklist.why: Kerf does not compute joint strength.

checklist.element: Bending and shear of the aprons and top
checklist.confirm: Confirm the aprons and top are strong enough, not only stiff enough.
checklist.why: There are no published design values for furniture lumber, so Kerf checks only deflection.
